finding.title: KI-0185 says a recurrence records both values, but WaitEmpty throws the values away
finding.claim: KI-0185 says 'Both refusals now name the two values, so a recurrence records them.' The phases KI-0185 lists as affected (forced-parent, quit, close) and Dispose all reach Members() only through WaitEmpty. WaitEmpty catches the 'Owned job list changing; assigned N, listed M' InvalidOperationException and drops its message, so a failing recurrence records neither value. The claim is false for exactly the case it describes.
finding.evidence: scripts/windows11/windows11_owned.cs:264 `try { members=Members(); } catch(InvalidOperationException error) { if(error is ObjectDisposedException) throw; }` keeps no last cause, and WaitEmpty just returns false at its deadline. The callers then throw fixed text: guest.ps1:287 'Native owned shutdown left job members', guest.ps1:479 'Owned foreground Ctrl+Q left owned job members after 6 s; ...', and owned.cs:708 Dispose 'Retained owned job failed to drain'. Elsewhere the code keeps the last 'not yet' cause for the deadline refusal: Settles uses settleLast and the PowerShell waits use LastTransient. WaitEmpty is the only bounded wait that does not.
finding.failure_scenario: Round 47 hv-5 repeats with a lasting mismatch. In the forced-parent phase, KillRoot runs, then Closed calls WaitEmpty(6000). Members() throws 'Owned job list changing; assigned 1, listed 0' on every poll for 6 s, WaitEmpty returns false, and failure.json records only 'Native owned shutdown left job members'. The assigned and listed values that KI-0185 says a recurrence now records are lost, and the message wrongly says members are left. Fix: keep the last transient message in WaitEmpty and expose it to the callers' refusals, or reword the KI.

2. Members() (scripts/windows11/windows11_owned.cs:211-225) throws two refusals that both carry the values:

3. WaitEmpty (owned.cs:260-268) has `try { members=Members(); } catch(InvalidOperationException error) { if(error is ObjectDisposedException) throw; }`. It drops the message, keeps no last cause, and only returns false at its deadline.
   - OwnedInvariantException is not an InvalidOperationException (owned.cs:14), so the overflow refusal still propagates with its values.

For the phases listed it is not.

- keep the last 'not yet' message in WaitEmpty and include it in the callers' refusals; or

I tried to refute this and could not. I checked the working tree directly.

- `WaitEmpty` (lines 260-268) catches the 'changing' refusal and keeps nothing from it: `try { members=Members(); } catch(InvalidOperationException error) { if(error is ObjectDisposedException) throw; }`. There is no last-cause variable and no out-parameter. At its deadline it just returns false.

- The accelerator check (line 479) and `Dispose` (owned.cs line 708, 'Retained owned job failed to drain') also throw fixed text.
- The finally-block cleanup records only `error_type` for a failed `Dispose`, with no message.

So neither recurrence case records the values:
- A brief count/list mismatch is retried and passes silently.
- A lasting mismatch fails at the 6 s deadline with fixed text that also wrongly says members were left.

The values do survive on other paths, and I checked them all:
- `Settles` keeps `settleLast`.
- The PowerShell waits keep `LastTransient`.
- A direct `Endpoint` call propagates the message to failure.json.

finding.title: The focus handoff can start after the 3 s settle deadline and then report the wrong cause
finding.claim: The deadline check runs only at the end of each iteration, followed by Thread.Sleep(10). An iteration can therefore begin past 3000 ms. The Math.Max(1, ...) floor then still starts a worker that does AttachThreadInput and SetFocus after the bound has expired, and joins it for only 1 ms. Join(1) almost always times out, so the refusal is 'Owned keyboard focus handoff did not return within its bound', which blames an unresponsive WebView2 thread. The real cause is that focus did not settle within 3 s. The orphaned worker then changes focus after SettleKeyboardFocus has already failed.
finding.evidence: Line 120: `HandFocus(focusThread,parent,(int)Math.Max(1,FocusSettleMilliseconds-watch.ElapsedMilliseconds));` runs before the deadline check at line 126. Line 145: `if(!worker.Join(milliseconds)) throw new InvalidOperationException("Owned keyboard focus handoff did not return within its bound");`. When remaining time is 0 or less, the floor gives 1 ms instead of skipping to the 'did not settle' refusal.
finding.failure_scenario: The end-of-iteration check runs at 2995 ms and passes. After Sleep(10), the next observation at about 3006 ms sees Chrome_RenderWidgetHostHWND with moves at 2 or less. HandFocus(...,1) starts a thread, Join(1) times out, and the phase fails with the handoff-bound message. The worker then calls SetFocus on Chrome_WidgetWin_1 after the failure. No false pass and no input is sent. The risk is a misdiagnosed failure and a focus change after the deadline. Fix: if remaining time is 0 or less, throw 'did not settle' instead of handing off.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not refute the finding. The code path exists as described, but its impact is minor.

How it happens, in scripts/windows11/windows11_owned.cs:
- SettleKeyboardFocus checks its deadline only at the end of each iteration (line 127), then sleeps 10 ms (line 128).
- So when the check at about 2995 ms passes, the next observation (lines 101-115) runs after 3000 ms.
- If that observation finds focus on Chrome_RenderWidgetHostHWND with at most two earlier handoffs, line 120 calls `HandFocus(focusThread,parent,(int)Math.Max(1,FocusSettleMilliseconds-watch.ElapsedMilliseconds))`. The floor turns zero or negative remaining time into 1 ms.
- The floor itself is deliberate. Join(-1) would wait forever and other negative values throw. But nothing skips the handoff when the time has already run out.
- HandFocus (lines 134-147) therefore starts a new worker that runs AttachThreadInput and SetFocus after the deadline, and waits for it with Join(1).

Two possible outcomes:
1. Join(1) times out. The phase fails with 'Owned keyboard focus handoff did not return within its bound', which points at an unresponsive WebView2 thread instead of 'Owned WebView2 keyboard focus did not settle'. The background worker can then still call SetFocus after the failure.
2. Join(1) returns in time. Then held=IntPtr.Zero (line 121), and line 127 throws the correct 'did not settle; last: Chrome_RenderWidgetHostHWND'. A focus change still happened after the deadline.

One overstatement in the finding: "Join(1) almost always times out" is not certain. Under PowerShell's default timer resolution of about 15.6 ms, a 1 ms wait can last longer. Either outcome is still a failure, so this does not change the conclusion.

Why it is not BLOCKING:
- **No false pass.** After any handoff, held is reset and the deadline check throws. A success return needs a quiet interval on the keyboard window (line 124).
- **No retry hides the failure.** Both exceptions are InvalidOperationException, but ShellKeys and KeyboardCheckAgain/KeyboardQuit are called directly in scripts/windows11/windows11_guest.ps1 (lines 215, 222, 232-234, 250-251, 255, 451, 478). They are not wrapped in a NotYet retry loop, so the exception fails the phase.
- **No input is sent.** SetFocus moves focus between two windows of the same owned WebView2 thread.
- **The overrun is small.** It is 1 ms plus timer granularity. The loop already overruns 3000 ms by up to one sleep and observation through its check-then-sleep design, which the repository's Settles helper shares (lines 329-336).

Related wording that is slightly imprecise:
- The KI-0184 resolution text (docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md line 87) says the handoff "is waited for only within the 3 s bound".
- The test comment at scripts/tests/test_windows11_guest_driver.py lines 858-859 says "only within what is left of the settle's own bound".
- Because of the 1 ms floor, a handoff that starts after the deadline is still waited for about 1 ms past it. The KI's real point, that an unresponsive WebView2 thread cannot hold the guest for long, still holds. So this is not a materially false recorded claim.

The fix is to throw 'did not settle' when the remaining time is zero or less, before calling HandFocus. That would also require updating the test that pins line 120.

I could not refute this finding. The code works as the finding describes. It is a real defect but a minor one.

How it happens (scripts/windows11/windows11_owned.cs, lines 98-147):
- In SettleKeyboardFocus, each iteration observes focus first. The deadline check at line 127 (`watch.ElapsedMilliseconds>=FocusSettleMilliseconds`) runs only after the observation, and then `Thread.Sleep(10)` follows.
- So the deadline check can pass at about 2995 ms, and the next observation can start past 3000 ms.
- If that observation finds focus on Chrome_RenderWidgetHostHWND, with the parent check passing and moves still at 3 or fewer, line 120 calls `HandFocus(focusThread,parent,(int)Math.Max(1,FocusSettleMilliseconds-watch.ElapsedMilliseconds))`. The floor turns a zero or negative remaining time into 1 ms.
- HandFocus then starts a new worker that runs AttachThreadInput and SetFocus after the bound has expired, and joins it with `Join(1)`.
- If the join times out, line 145 throws 'Owned keyboard focus handoff did not return within its bound'. The real cause is that focus did not settle within 3 s. The background worker is left running and may change Win32 focus after the phase has already failed.
- If the join succeeds, line 121 clears `held`, line 127 throws the correct 'did not settle' message, but a SetFocus has still been issued past the deadline.

One correction to the finding: 'Join(1) almost always times out' is overstated. At Windows' default ~15.6 ms timer resolution, a 1 ms wait can last up to one clock tick, so a responsive WebView2 thread often finishes the handoff in time. In that case the message is correct and only the post-deadline SetFocus remains. The misattribution happens only some of the time.

Why it is not blocking:
- Once HandFocus is entered past the deadline, the call always fails: either line 145 throws, or `held` is cleared and line 127 throws. It cannot cause a false pass.
- No input is sent. SetFocus is not SendInput, and the target is the owned WebView2 keyboard window that was already checked against the parent, same thread, same process and member rules.
- Both possible messages are InvalidOperationException. ShellKeys and Keys are called directly in the keyboard phase of scripts/windows11/windows11_guest.ps1 (lines 215-255 and 451/478), not inside a NotYet retry loop. Either throw therefore fails the phase closed. The stray worker cannot affect a retried attempt.
- Leaving a worker running after a join timeout is already part of the design for a WebView2 thread that stops responding. The extra wait past the deadline is only the 1 ms join, rounded up to at most one clock tick.

Recorded claims:
- The KI-0184 sentence in docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md says the handoff 'is waited for only within the 3 s bound, so a WebView2 thread that stops responding cannot hold the guest past it'. That is slightly imprecise at this edge, since a handoff can start after the deadline and be waited on for about one tick. The guest still cannot be held materially past the bound, so I do not count it as a false claim.
- The test comment at scripts/tests/test_windows11_guest_driver.py (around line 858, 'only within what is left of the settle's own bound') has the same imprecision.

Suggested fix: if the remaining time is 0 or less, refuse with 'did not settle' instead of calling HandFocus.

finding.title: initial_startup_timeout doc comment says the first start fails on every VM without Hyper-V enlightenments, but retained evidence has a counterexample
finding.claim: The comment begins 'On nested Windows 11 VMs without Hyper-V enlightenments, the first start missed the 10 s bound'. Read plainly, that says it happens on every such VM. KI-0182 itself makes the narrower claim: it names three VMs (round 40 ignore-terminal, round 42 host-terminal, round 44 host-nowhesvc). The retained evidence includes a VM without enlightenments whose desktop first start met the 10 s bound.
finding.evidence: round43-41686846768/svcfirst__qemu-argv.json uses '-cpu host' with no hv-* flags and the same package_sha256 5700fefc... as the hv variant. Its diag-progress.txt has 'launched at_ms=64171' and 'ready-ok at_ms=76490'. Its diag-ready.ndjson shows the bare title 'Desktop App' (RecoveryState::Running) at 73310 ms, about 9.1 s after launch. That run came after the standalone cold service start (service-cold-done at_ms=61333), which warmed the binaries. So the qualifier the comment leaves out is 'cold first start', or 'three VMs'. The other figures in the comment do match the evidence. Round 42 host-terminal diag-procs.txt has the desktop absent at t_ms=4147 and present at 6279, and japp-orchestrator absent at 10737 and present at 12959, which gives 4458 to 8812 ms (4.5 to 8.8 s). Round 43 diag-service-cold.json has first_bytes_ms=7603, and the round 43 guest-driver diff shows that stopwatch starts just before Process.Start, so 'READY 7.6 s after its spawn began' is right.
finding.failure_scenario: A later reader or reviewer takes 'without Hyper-V enlightenments' alone as the trigger for the first-start failure. Round 43 svcfirst, retained in this change, contradicts that. Rewording to 'in three cold first launches on nested VMs without Hyper-V enlightenments (KI-0182)' would make the comment match KI-0182 and the evidence. This does not affect behavior.

finding.title: KI-0179 worst-case budget margin 'more than 50 s' leaves out the attestor-to-environment time
finding.claim: 'With the attestor at the 150 s mark (its worst case), that leaves more than 50 s of the 300 s budget.' The retained evidence does not support this. The sum only works if the environment receipt arrives as soon as the attestor wait ends.
finding.evidence: In scripts/windows11/windows11_guest.ps1 (lines 354-430), the guest waits for the attestor (until the 150 s mark at worst), then runs the receipt checks and the owned dxdiag (WaitEmpty up to 45 s), and only then writes the environment receipt. In every enlightened VM with a dxdiag measurement, the owned dxdiag alone took 19.5 to 22.7 s (diag-dxdiag-owned.txt, rounds 43-46: 19493, 21563, 20181, 20073, 21345, 19804, 22688, 22267, 21635 ms). Environment came at 21.7-29.7 s in those rounds and at 25.7-27.6 s in round 48, so the attestor itself finished within the first few seconds. The KI text's own range is that round 48 took 85.8-96.3 s from environment to cleanup. Worst case is therefore about 150 + ~20 + 85.8..96.3 = 255-266 s, which leaves about 34-45 s. That is below 50 s even for the fastest VM. The '>50 s' figure comes from 300 - 150 - 96.3 = 53.7, which drops the dxdiag interval.
finding.failure_scenario: An owner sizing the guest budget from this KI believes there is >50 s of headroom at the attestor's worst case. The measured headroom is about 34-45 s, so a slower first logon or a later phase growth of 35-45 s would overrun the 300 s deadline although the KI says it should not.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not refute this. The finding holds against both the code and the retained evidence.

Code order (scripts/windows11/windows11_guest.ps1). `$clock` starts at line 4. The attestor wait loops `while($clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds -lt 150)` (lines 354-366), so in the worst case it ends at about 150 s. After that the guest:
1. Retains the receipts and trace.
2. Runs the mismatch and hardware checks.
3. Runs the owned dxdiag: `StartCommand` then `WaitEmpty(45000)` (lines 412-416).
4. Writes environment.json and only then `Receipt 'environment'` (line 430).

So in the worst case, the environment receipt comes at 150 s plus the post-attestor work, not at 150 s.

The diagnostic drivers in the evidence keep that order. The round 45 guest-driver-vs-2100780.diff adds a dxdiag stopwatch around the same owned `StartCommand`/`WaitEmpty`, which comes after the machine wait.

Retained owned-dxdiag times in the nine enlightened VMs (`diag-dxdiag-owned.txt`, `job_empty_ms`):
- Round 43 hv: 19493 ms.
- Round 44 hv-b and hv-nowhesvc: 21563 and 20181 ms.
- Round 45 hv-1/2/3: 20073, 21345 and 19804 ms.
- Round 46 hv-1/2/4: 22688, 22267 and 21635 ms.

In those VMs the environment receipt came at 21.7 to 29.7 s (receipts.ndjson). The time from the attestor wait ending to the environment receipt is therefore about 20 s, not about 0.

Round 48 receipts confirm the KI's own figures:
- Environment at 25.7 to 27.6 s and cleanup at 111.5 to 123.2 s.
- Environment to cleanup: 94.4, 94.5, 92.2, 96.3 and 85.8 s, so 85.8 to 96.3 s.

The worst-case arithmetic:
- The KI's "more than 50 s" only follows from 300 - 150 - 96.3 = 53.7 s. That needs the stretch from the attestor wait ending to the environment receipt (mostly dxdiag) to take under 3.7 s, and no retained evidence shows that.
- With the measured dxdiag included, the margin is about 300 - (150 + 19.5..22.7 + 85.8..96.3) = 31 to 45 s, below 50 s even for the fastest VM.
- Round 48 has no dxdiag measurement of its own. Its environment at 25.7 to 27.6 s caps that stretch at 27.6 s, which still allows a margin as low as about 26 s.

The claim at docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md:184 is a derived number that the retained evidence does not support. Measured headroom is about 31 to 45 s, so the stated "more than 50 s" is false. Under the binding rules (a false recorded claim; recorded numbers must match retained evidence) this is BLOCKING. It is a documentation-only defect: no code behavior is wrong.

finding.title: Round 43 'lost key' classification is inferred, not measured
finding.claim: KI-0184 says nine of ten keyboard-phase VMs in rounds 43-46 failed because 'a fixed Tab or Enter ... had no effect', counting 'all four in rounds 43 and 44'. The README round 43 row (line 262) says 'Both VMs that reached the keyboard phase lost a key there'.
finding.evidence: Round 43 hv and svcfirst kept only failure.json ('Actual bounded native shell focus or geometry did not settle') and diag-foreground.txt. Round 43 has no diag-waits.txt and no diag-focus.txt. Its ShellWait bound was the normal 3 s (round 43 guest-driver diff line 170). The 30 s diagnostic bounds and the per-wait records that show 'no effect' start in round 44.
finding.failure_scenario: A reader takes the round 43 failures as measured lost keys. The retained round 43 evidence only shows a 3 s shell wait timing out, which a settle longer than 3 s would also produce.

verdicts.reasoning:
I could not refute the finding. It is real, and it is a minor wording-precision issue.

Every evidence point in the finding checks out:
- Round 43 kept only failure.json, guest-terminal.json and diag-foreground.txt for the two VMs that reached the keyboard phase (hv and svcfirst). There is no diag-waits.txt and no diag-focus.txt.
- Both failures carry the message "Actual bounded native shell focus or geometry did not settle" with no transient suffix.
- The ShellWait in round 43 (guest-driver-vs-2100780.diff line 170) is `$clock.Elapsed.TotalSeconds+3`, so the bound was 3 s.
- The 30 s diagnostic bound first appears in round 44 (round 44 diff line 193: `+30) # DIAG: measure, was 3`). Round 44's diag-waits.txt is the first to record failed waits of about 29.6 to 29.9 s. The resend-for-a-minute measurement is round 46.

What the round 43 evidence does support:
- Both failures happened exactly where KI-0184 says keys are lost. I mapped the OwnForeground log against the guest sequence; ShellFocusRoute, ShellFocusSkip and ShellKeys each log one shell acknowledgment, and ShellRouteGeometry logs none.
- hv: 56 entries, ending with the diagnostics capture, the Check-again keyboard acknowledgment, then ShellFocusSkip and ShellKeys('enter'). The run then failed in `ShellWait { ShellMainFocused }`.
- svcfirst: 27 entries, failing at the same wait after the Tracker route.
- So each failure was a fixed Enter sent straight after a UIA SetFocus whose effect did not appear within 3 s. That is consistent with the mechanism measured in round 47.
- KI-0184's phrase "had no effect" is literally true for round 43 within its 3 s window.

Why the finding still stands:
- The README round 43 row (line 262) says "Both VMs that reached the keyboard phase lost a key there". KI-0184 counts "all four in rounds 43 and 44" among keys that "had no effect", followed in the same paragraph by the round 46 minute-long resend result.
- For round 43, "lost" means the key never took effect, and that is inferred, not measured. A settle longer than 3 s would leave the same retained record.
- The gap is wider for svcfirst. It ran plain `-cpu host` (svcfirst__qemu-argv.json) with no Hyper-V enlightenments. Settle times on `-cpu host` were never measured, and the 24 to 426 ms success range comes only from round 44's enlightened VMs.
- Against that, svcfirst's earlier ShellMainFocused waits after the same skip-link Enter (Home and Jobs) did succeed within 3 s. So a slow settle is unlikely, but the retained round 43 data cannot exclude it.

Severity: NON_BLOCKING. The VM counts (2+2+2+3 = 9 of 10) and the failure locations are accurate. The mechanism attribution is well supported by later rounds, and nothing in the gating logic depends on the round 43 label. Two small fixes would correct it:
- Qualify round 43 as "the post-Enter focus did not settle within the normal 3 s bound".
- Scope the "lost" (no effect over 30 to 60 s) wording to rounds 44 to 46.

I could not refute the finding. The retained round 43 evidence supports the reviewer's description of it.

What round 43 kept:
- Round 43 evidence directory: docs/evidence/m03-native-runtime-diagnostics/windows-rehearsal-rounds/round43-41686846768.
- The two VMs that reached the keyboard phase are hv and svcfirst. Both kept only failure.json and guest-terminal.json, each with the ShellWait message 'Actual bounded native shell focus or geometry did not settle'. They also kept diag-foreground.txt, which lists foreground requests, plus progress, receipt and ready files.
- Neither VM has diag-waits.txt, diag-focus.txt or a failure frame.
- The round 43 guest-driver-vs-2100780.diff kept ShellWait at '+3' (3 s). The 30 s diagnostic bounds ('# DIAG: measure, was 3') and the per-wait diag-waits.txt records first appear in round 44.

What the round 43 evidence can and cannot show:
- I counted the foreground-request lines against ShellCapture's call sequence. Each Snapshot is one 'capture' line. ShellFocusRoute, tab, backtab and enter are four shell acknowledgments, and ShellFocusSkip plus enter are two. Counted this way, hv (56 lines) failed at the ShellMainFocused wait after the skip Enter on the baseline Diagnostics route, and svcfirst (27 lines) failed at the same wait after Tracker.
- So both failures came at a ShellWait right after a key that followed a UIA focus request. That matches KI-0184's mechanism.
- The only measurement, though, is that a 3 s wait expired. A focus settle slower than 3 s would leave the same record. Round 43 has nothing showing the key 'had no effect': no long wait, no resend and no Win32 focus record.

Where the docs overstate it:
- docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md line 78 says nine of ten keyboard-phase VMs failed because a fixed Tab or Enter 'had no effect', and counts 'all four in rounds 43 and 44'.
- README line 262 says round 43's two VMs 'lost a key there'.
- Both state the round 43 classification as a measured fact without saying it is inferred. Elsewhere this changeset labels inferences explicitly: KI-0185 ('not recorded, so neither the cause ... was measured') and KI-0175 ('an inference, not a measurement').

Why NON_BLOCKING:
- The classification is very probably right. In round 44, with 30 s bounds, every successful ShellWait took 24 to 426 ms, and both failing waits ran to about 29.6 to 29.9 s with ok=False.
- The defect and its correction rest on rounds 44 to 48, which were measured directly: 30 s waits, resends and focus traces.
- No threshold, gate state or correction depends on the two round 43 cases.

The fix is to label the round 43 count as inferred from a 3 s ShellWait timeout at the same step. It is not a false or load-bearing claim.
